parole.significato: placename suffix found in Alsace, Lorraine, and adjacent areas of eastern France
parole.testo: From Alemannic German -wiler, from Middle High German wīler, wīlære (“hamlet, farmstead”), from Old High German wīlāri (“hamlet, farmstead”), from Latin villāre (“farmstead, manor”). Cognate with German Weiler, Old French viller.

parole.significato: a cafe, restaurant or bar that specialises in beer
parole.testo: From Alsatian Alemannic German Bierstub f, cognate to German Bierstube.

From earlier bivoie, biouac, bivac, from Alemannic German Biiwacht (“a patrol of citizens added - in time of alarm or commotion - to the regular town watch”), from bii- (“by-”) + Wacht (“watch, guard”).

parole.significato: bredele (a biscuit or small cake traditionally eaten in the Christmas period in Alsace and Moselle, France)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Alemannic German bredele, diminutive of brot (“bread”).
From Alemannic German Kakel (compare Standard German Kachel) + -on.
Borrowed from Alemannic German schneck (“snail”) (compare Standard German Schnecke).
From Alemannic German (Alsatian) Schoppe, which is related to German schoppen (“to tuck”). Compare modern German Schoppen.

parole.significato: sauerkraut (a dish made by fermenting finely chopped cabbage)
parole.testo: From Alsatian Alemannic German surkrut, Surkrut, Sürkrut (standard German Sauerkraut). The first part of the word was modified by folk etymology to French chou (“cabbage”). Since -croute (krut, German Kraut) is that part of the Germanic word that indeed means “cabbage”, the French form quite literal
Attested from 1671, originally as sible. Originally Swiss French, borrowed from Alemannic German Schiibe or rather the diminutive Schiibli; compare German Scheibe.
From Alsatian Alemannic German fristick (standard German Frühstück).
Uncertain, perhaps from Alemannic German granggel, gränggeli.

parole.significato: kepi (cap with a flat circular top)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Alemannic German Käppi, compare German Kappe.
